sections.h2: Where is Lafayette, Indiana, and what shapes its housing?
sections.html:
Lafayette is the county seat of Tippecanoe County, on the southeast bank of the Wabash River, directly across from West Lafayette. It sits about 63 miles northwest of Indianapolis and 125 miles southeast of Chicago, at an elevation of roughly 663 feet.

The city covers close to 29.5 square miles. Most of it lies in Fairfield and Wea Townships, which matters when you read a tax bill or a deed. The 2020 census counted 70,783 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 71,238, so the housing stock is mostly built out rather than spreading fast.

The river sets the shape of the town. Older streets run downhill toward the water, newer subdivisions sit on the plateau and the outer edges, and Purdue University across the bridge pulls renters and investors into the same market as long-time owners.

Lafayette was platted by William Digby in May 1825 and named for the Marquis de Lafayette. A year later it became the seat of the newly formed Tippecanoe County, and it was incorporated in 1853.

Earlier, the French built Fort Ouiatenon in 1717 about three miles south, across the Wabash. The 1840s brought the Wabash and Erie Canal, and the 1850s brought railroads, including the Monon. On August 17, 1859, balloonist John Wise lifted off from the courthouse grounds carrying what is recorded as the first official U.S. airmail delivery.

That age shows up in the houses. Houses in the historic neighborhoods can carry the repair needs that come with age, and that is a common reason an owner decides repairs are not worth chasing before a sale.

Lafayette has more than two dozen named neighborhoods, and the age and condition of a house usually follow the neighborhood. Names on the city's list include Ninth Street Hill, Centennial, Columbian Park, Downtown, Ellsworth Romig, Glen Acres, Hanna, Hedgewood, Highland Park, Jefferson, Linnwood, Monon, Orchard Heights, Perrin, Potter Hollow, St. Mary's, Valley Center, Vinton, Wabash and Wallace Triangle.

  • Historic districts include Ninth Street Hill and Upper Main Street, plus Downtown, Ellsworth, Highland Park, Jefferson, Perrin and St. Mary's.
  • Older core neighborhoods are where the historic districts sit.
  • Outer neighborhoods such as Vinton Highlands and Jesco Hills Estates were developed later.

If your house is inside a historic district, check with the city before you plan exterior work. For a buyer who purchases as-is, that question moves to the buyer.

Manufacturing and Purdue drive the local job market. The city's industrial employers include Wabash National, which is described as the world's largest semi-truck trailer maker, and Subaru of Indiana Automotive, the only non-Japanese plant producing Subaru vehicles.

Other plants named for the area are Evonik's Tippecanoe Laboratories, Primient's corn processing operation, Landis+Gyr and a Caterpillar large engine center. At the county level, Purdue is described as by far the largest employer, followed by Subaru, Wabash National, Caterpillar, Alcoa, State Farm and several hospitals.

For a seller, this means demand for housing is tied to plant shifts and the academic calendar. A job change or a transfer out of town is one of the most common reasons owners here want a quick sale.

sections.h2: What is the weather like, and what does it do to a house?
sections.html:
Lafayette has cold winters and warm, humid summers. Normals for 1991 to 2020 at a nearby station show an average January low of 17.7 degrees F, an average July high of 83.6 degrees F, about 39.8 inches of precipitation a year and 20.5 inches of snow.

Freeze and thaw cycles are hard on roofs, gutters, chimneys and driveways, and heating costs matter in the old housing stock.

The Wabash is the other factor. The USGS has published flood inundation maps for about 4.8 miles of the river at Lafayette, built from the gage record and the high water marks of the July 2003 flood. The maps show how far water spreads at each river stage. If your house is near the river, look up the flood zone, because insurance requirements and a buyer's lender will ask the same question.

sections.h2: How do you get around Lafayette?
sections.html:
Interstate 65, U.S. 52, U.S. 231 and State Roads 25, 26 and 38 serve the city. The nearest commercial airport is Purdue University Airport in West Lafayette, and Amtrak's Cardinal stops in town on its Chicago to New York route.

  • CityBus, run by the Greater Lafayette Public Transportation Corporation, covers the city and West Lafayette.
  • Greyhound and FlixBus connect Lafayette to Chicago and Indianapolis.
  • Shuttle services run to Indianapolis International and O'Hare.

Commuters to Indianapolis use I-65, which keeps Lafayette within reach of a second job market.

Lafayette School Corporation serves most of the city and runs Jefferson High School. Tippecanoe School Corporation serves outlying areas and operates McCutcheon High School and William Henry Harrison High School.

Which district a house falls into depends on the address, so confirm with the district rather than assuming from the mailing city. Private options include Catholic Central Junior-Senior High School, Lafayette Christian School and Faith Christian School.

sections.h2: What local rules affect a Lafayette sale or rental?
sections.html:
Lafayette's rules center on permits and short-term rentals. According to the city's FAQ page, permits are generally required for property modifications, though routine maintenance, non-structural reroofing and landscaping are exempt.

  • A shed on a permanent foundation, or over 120 square feet, needs a building permit and must meet setbacks.
  • Fences do not need a permit, but residential fences in a street frontage setback are capped at 42 inches.
  • Short-term rentals fall under Ordinance 2017-27, and a $100 application fee was set by Ordinance 2018-01 for the transient rental registration permit.
  • The city does not survey property lines, so a surveyor is the answer to boundary doubts.

Owners of dead trees on private land are responsible for them. Unpermitted work is worth disclosing to any buyer.

sections.h2: How are a deed and transfer handled in Tippecanoe County?
sections.html:
A deed must go through the County Assessor and Auditor before the Recorder will record it, and the Assessor requires a sales disclosure form filed first. The Tippecanoe County Recorder is on the second floor of the County Office Building at 20 North 3rd Street.

Under Indiana Code 6-1.1-5.5-3, the parties to a conveyance complete the form before the document goes to the auditor, and the assessor must approve it first. One form covers contiguous parcels in one taxing district on a single deed.

The recorder lists hours of Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and sets fees under Indiana Code 36-2-7-10.2. A title or escrow company normally handles all of this at closing.

sections.h2: When are Tippecanoe County property taxes due?
sections.html:
Indiana property tax is due in two installments, on May 10 and November 10. For 2026 the Tippecanoe County Treasurer listed May 11 and November 10 as the due dates.

The Treasurer's office is at 20 N 3rd Street, 2nd Floor, Lafayette, open weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Mailed payments must be federally postmarked by the deadline, and meter dates are not accepted.

If you are selling mid-year, ask the closing agent how the taxes will be prorated so there are no surprises on the settlement statement. The state tax guide linked on this page explains appeals and deductions.

sections.h2: What do Lafayette sellers usually face?
sections.html:
Owners here most often sell because of inherited homes, tenant problems, out-of-town moves, deferred repairs or mounting payments. An older house in a historic neighborhood may need foundation, plumbing and roof work that costs more than a listing would recover.

  • Listing with an agent means preparing, showing and waiting on a buyer's financing and inspection.
  • Selling yourself saves the commission but puts marketing and paperwork on you.
  • A cash buyer purchases the house as it is, and you pick the closing date.

Compare each option on net proceeds and timing, not the headline number alone. You can request a cash offer and compare it to the others with no obligation.

faqs.q: Do I need to repair my Lafayette house before selling for cash?
faqs.a: No. A cash buyer purchases the house in its current condition, so repairs, cleaning and staging are not required. You can still disclose known problems, which keeps the sale clean.

faqs.q: Which county is Lafayette in, and who records the deed?
faqs.a: Lafayette is in Tippecanoe County. The Tippecanoe County Recorder, at 20 North 3rd Street, records deeds after the Assessor and Auditor process the sales disclosure form.

faqs.q: When are Tippecanoe County property taxes due?
faqs.a: State law sets May 10 and November 10. In 2026 the county Treasurer listed May 11 and November 10, and mailed payments must be federally postmarked by the deadline.

faqs.q: Does Lafayette require a permit for short-term rentals?
faqs.a: Yes. Short-term rentals are regulated under city Ordinance 2017-27, and a $100 application fee was set for a transient rental registration permit. Check with the city for current details.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Lafayette house that sits near the Wabash River?
faqs.a: Yes. A buyer or lender may check the flood zone, and USGS flood inundation maps cover about 4.8 miles of the river at Lafayette. A cash buyer can still purchase the house as-is.

faqs.q: How long does a cash sale in Lafayette take?
faqs.a: It depends on title work and the closing date you choose. Because there is no buyer mortgage to approve, timing mostly follows the title work and your chosen closing date.
